Our vendor's benchmark shows their library is 'up to 8x faster'. Our trial showed about 20%. What games produce that gap?

Several classics, all legal under the phrase 'up to'. Best-of-many reporting: run the benchmark a hundred times, publish the single fastest run for their code and a typical or worst run for the competitor's. Cherry-picked workload: the 8x is real for one input shape (huge inputs, one specific operation, data that fits a cache trick) and the other shapes, including yours, are unremarkable. Warm-versus-cold asymmetry: their code measured after warmup, yours including startup. Different work entirely: their path skips validation, error handling, or a copy that the production path cannot skip, so the benchmark compares a engine without the car built around it.

There is also the quietest trick: measuring in a regime where the constant they optimized dominates, then letting you assume it scales. An 8x win on a microbenchmark of a 200-nanosecond operation buys you nothing inside a 50-millisecond request.

Your defense is procedural, and your 20% trial already applied it: benchmark on your workload, your data sizes, your hardware, end to end, with the full production path doing the full production work. Treat vendor numbers as a hypothesis about where to look, never as evidence. And when you publish your own benchmarks someday, the same standard is what makes them credible: workload described, distribution reported, worst case included. 'Up to' is doing all the work in that sentence; make vendors say 'typically, on workloads like yours', or do the measuring yourself.
I made our parser 15% faster by replacing clear code with a hand-rolled state machine that's hard to read. The parser is 4% of our runtime. My reviewer wants me to revert. Who's right?

Your reviewer, and Amdahl's law is the whole argument: 15% faster on a component that is 4% of runtime improves the total by about 0.6%. You have traded a permanent readability cost, paid by every future reader and every future bug fix in that file, for a benefit no user can perceive and no dashboard can reliably distinguish from noise. The exchange rate is terrible.

This is the arithmetic most optimization debates skip. The value of a local speedup is the local saving multiplied by the component's share of the whole. Teams feel the 15% because it is attached to their code and their effort; the system feels the 0.6%. Before optimizing anything, multiply: if share times saving is under a percent, the only honest justification is that the code was getting clearer anyway.

There are narrow exceptions: if the parser is about to become 40% of runtime because a planned feature multiplies its traffic tenfold, optimizing now can be foresight, but then the review should say that, with the projection attached, and the readability cost should be mitigated with comments explaining the machine and tests pinning its behavior. Absent that story, revert, and keep the clear version. Bank the knowledge of how to make it faster in a comment or a note; if the profile ever promotes the parser into the critical few percent, you will know exactly what to do, and then it will be worth doing.
Before I adopt a micro-optimization I saw in a blog, what should I check? It promises 30% on a common operation.

Check four things, in order. First, the baseline: 30% of what, measured how, on which version of the language? Micro-optimizations are the most perishable goods in programming; a trick that won on an old interpreter can be neutral or negative on a current one, because the runtime's own optimizations move underneath them. If the post does not name its environment and method, it is folklore, not data.

Second, your own profile: does the operation it speeds up appear in your hot path at a share worth having? Thirty percent of an operation that is 1% of your runtime is 0.3%, beneath notice. Third, measure it yourself, on your code, with your data sizes, in a harness that repeats and reports a distribution; blog benchmarks are tuned to the blog's example, and the gap between their snippet and your loop is where promised percentages go to die. Fourth, price the readability: if the optimized form is a line longer or a trick the next reader must puzzle out, the saving must be large and proven, not small and rumored.

Adopt only if all four pass: current evidence, a hot path that includes the operation, your own measurement confirming a worthwhile margin, and a clarity cost you are willing to document. That sounds like a lot of ceremony for a small change, and it is deliberately so: micro-optimizations are individually tiny and collectively a fog that settles over a codebase. The ceremony is what keeps the fog out.

When is using more memory the right way to go faster, and when is it a trap?

It is right when the memory buys the elimination of repeated work and the trade is made with open eyes: a cache that turns a database round trip into a lookup, a precomputed table that turns a per-request calculation into an array read, an index that spends disk to make queries logarithmic. In each case you can state the exchange rate (this many bytes for that many operations saved) and the memory is bounded by something you control.

It is a trap in three recurring shapes. First, when the memory grows with the input while the patience of the machine does not: an optimization that holds everything in RAM is a bet that inputs stay under a cliff, and cliffs are discovered in production. Second, when the memory pressure evicts the system's other caches: your structure grows, the OS page cache and the CPU caches shrink around it, and code you did not touch gets slower, a cost that never appears in your microbenchmark. Third, when the memory is spent to avoid a computation that was not actually the bottleneck, which buys nothing at any price.

The discipline is to treat memory as a budget with a stated source: how much, growing with what, bounded by what, and evicting how. If you can answer those four for a proposed structure, it is an engineering trade. If the answer is 'it holds what it holds', it is a trap on a timer. Speed bought with unbounded memory is rented, and the rent comes due at the worst scale, on the worst day.

A `__slots__` class reserves the two fields in the object itself and has no dict at all: in this measurement the per-instance cost falls from 344 bytes to 48. The case for slots is specifically 'millions of instances of a fixed shape', which is exactly your case.

Programmers estimate an object's size as its payload (two numbers: sixteen bytes) and forget the container tax the runtime charges per instance. At small counts the tax is invisible; at large counts it is the budget. Our job got slower gradually for months, then fell off a cliff last week and now takes 40x longer. Nothing in the code changed. What kind of cause does that?

That signature, gradual decline then a cliff, is the classic shape of a resource crossing a capacity threshold, and memory is the usual suspect. While the working set fits in RAM, growth costs a little: more pages touched, worse cache locality, longer GC pauses. The week the working set exceeds physical memory, the operating system begins swapping, and every access pattern that was merely inefficient becomes a disk operation. Disk is not a slower tier of memory in any gentle sense; it is four to five orders of magnitude slower, so a job does not get 40% slower at the cliff, it gets 40x slower, exactly as yours did.

Other cliffs have the same silhouette: a table outgrowing a cache so a query plan flips from index to scan, a log or queue crossing the size where it stops fitting in the page cache, a data structure whose resizing or rehashing changes character at a threshold. The diagnostic method is to find what grew and what it crossed. Plot the job's input size and memory use over the months; the cliff week will line up with a capacity number (RAM, a cache size, a buffer limit) being reached.

The management lesson is to monitor headroom, not just duration. A job at 60% of RAM growing 2% a month has a calculable cliff date, and capacity work is cheap when scheduled and miserable when discovered. Gradual-then-sudden is never a mystery once you ask 'what filled up'; something always did. Find the container, watch its level, and treat 80% full as the incident, months before the cliff makes it one for you.

At what point does a memory problem stop being tunable and force us to redesign the job as streaming?

The line is crossed when the data's size is controlled by the world rather than by you, and it exceeds any memory you can budget. Tuning works while the working set can be made to fit: compress the representation, store columns instead of objects, evict colder data. Those are constant-factor defenses, and they lose to unbounded growth exactly the way faster constants lose to worse exponents. If input size doubles yearly and your representation merely halves the footprint, you have bought one year.

Streaming is the redesign that changes the exponent of memory: instead of proportional to the input, memory becomes proportional to a window, a batch, or the largest single record. The tells that you need it: the job's memory graph tracks its input graph, failures are out-of-memory kills at peak input, and every capacity conversation ends with 'buy a bigger box', which is a plan with an expiration date and a procurement department.

The redesign is usually less total than feared, because most batch jobs are secretly streamable: records are processed independently, aggregations are incremental, outputs are append-only. The work is finding the places that secretly required everything at once (a global sort, a join against the full set, a distinct-count over all history) and giving each an explicit strategy: external sort, windowed join, approximate distinct count. Cross the line deliberately, while the system still works, and the redesign is a project. Cross it when the cliff arrives, and it is an incident with a project inside it.

Reserve wall-clock budgets for dedicated or quiet environments, with generous thresholds that catch cliffs rather than jitter.

The cultural half matters as much as the tooling. A regression budget only works if a red performance test is treated as a real failure, not a flaky annoyance to be retried into green; the first time a team waves one through, the suite becomes decoration. And when a regression is intentional (a correctness fix that costs speed, a feature that adds work), the budget gets updated in the same commit, with the reason in the message. How do I know when to STOP optimizing? There's always another percent somewhere.

The first stop is the spec: if the system meets its stated budget (latency, throughput, operation counts) with headroom for expected growth, further speed has no customer. The second stop is the profile's floor: when the remaining time is spread thin across dozens of small contributors with no dominant one, the era of profitable optimization is over; you are in the long tail where each change buys a fraction of a percent at full price. The third stop is economic: when the next optimization's engineering cost exceeds the value of the capacity or latency it returns, which you can often compute surprisingly literally (engineer-weeks against server-months, or against the revenue sensitivity of the latency).

What replaces optimizing, at the stop, is protecting: budgets in CI so the level you reached is defended automatically, and a note in the file recording what was tried and what the profile looked like, so the next person does not re-derive it.

The mindset shift is from 'faster is better' to 'fast enough, verifiably, is a feature'. A system at its budget with clear code and guarded performance is a finished system. A system 3% faster with a hairball where the parser used to be is a liability that happens to benchmark well. Know which one you are building, and let the budget, not the itch, call the stop.

Here is the whole method in one small program, with nothing waved. Step one, instrument before touching: the counters divide the work into parse (2,000 operations, one per line, exactly as expected), rate lookups (about 41,000), and render (1). Step two, read the shape, not the vibes: the lookup count is twenty times the parse count because each of the 2,000 records scans the rates list until it matches, averaging half the list. That is a nested scan, a hand-written join, and it owns the operation census. Parse and render are arithmetically innocent whatever their code looks like.

Step three, change exactly that one thing: build a dict from the rates once, and let each record resolve its rate with a single probe. The parse logic is untouched, the render step is untouched, the arithmetic is untouched. Step four, prove all three claims an optimization must prove: the target operation collapsed (roughly 41,000 scans to 2,000 lookups), the bystanders did not move (parse still 2,000, render still 1), and the answer is identical (same total), so behavior is preserved and only cost changed.

Notice what this diagnosis never needed: a stopwatch. Operation counts carried the entire argument, which is why they are the first instrument to reach for; they are exact, portable, and they point at causes rather than symptoms. When counts cannot see the cost (I/O waits, lock contention, cache effects), then you bring in timers and profilers, in that order. Profile, hypothesize, change one thing, prove it three ways. That loop, repeated, is the entire discipline; everything else in performance work is commentary.
